v.why: Edge 2 reaches the output only through edge 5, so when edge 5 is none the edit is disconnected and its usual positive gain shrinks to zero.
Edge 1 feeds node 2, which reaches the output only via edge 5, so with edge 5 removed the usually helpful conv upgrade has no path to the output.
Replacing an empty edge with a 3x3 conv adds a whole learnable path, whereas replacing an existing op gives a smaller gain.
Upgrading an already strong conv1x1 yields a marginal gain compared with upgrading a skip, pool or none edge.
Replacing a strong 3x3 conv with a parameter-free skip loses much more accuracy than replacing a weak op.
Removing a strong direct conv edge hurts more than removing a weak or already empty one, so the signed effect is more negative.
Pooling in place of an empty output edge adds a usable path, while pooling in place of a conv discards learned capacity.
Swapping a strong conv for a non-learnable pool on an output-adjacent edge costs more than swapping a weak op, and this loss shows especially on low-resolution data.
Cutting the early input edge when it is a strong conv removes the main feature extractor for downstream edges, a bigger loss than removing a weak op.
Filling an empty direct input-to-output edge with a conv adds a short trainable path, a larger gain than replacing an op that already contributes.

| 9 | edge 0 → none | edge 0 = nor_conv_3x3 | self-conditioning | negative | lower |
| 10 | edge 3 → nor_conv_1x1 | edge 3 = none | self-conditioning | positive | higher |
